{{Short description|Algebraic construction}}
{{Ring theory sidebar}}
In [[mathematics]], the '''ring of integers''' of an [[algebraic number field]] <math>K</math> (also sometimes called the '''number ring''' corresponding to number field ''<math>K</math>'')<ref>{{Cite book |last=Marcus |first=Daniel A. |title=Number fields |date=2018 |publisher=Springer |others=Emanuele Sacco |isbn=978-3-319-90232-6 |edition=2nd |series=Universitext |location=Cham}}</ref> is the [[ring (mathematics)|ring]] of all [[algebraic integer]]s contained in <math>K</math>.{{sfn|Alaca|Williams|2003|loc=Defs. 6.1.2-3|p=110}} An algebraic integer is a [[root of a polynomial|root]] of a [[monic polynomial]] with [[integer]] [[coefficient]]s: <math>x^n+c_{n-1}x^{n-1}+\cdots+c_0</math>.{{sfn|Alaca|Williams|2003|loc=Defs. 4.1.1-2|p=74}} This ring is often denoted by <math>O_K</math> or <math>\mathcal O_K</math>. Since any [[integer]] belongs to <math>K</math> and is an [[integral element]] of <math>K</math>, the ring <math>\mathbb{Z}</math> is always a [[subring]] of <math>O_K</math>.

The ring of integers <math>\mathbb{Z}</math> is the simplest possible ring of integers.{{efn|''The ring of integers'', without specifying the field, refers to the ring <math>\mathbb{Z}</math> of "ordinary" integers, the prototypical object for all those rings. It is a consequence of the ambiguity of the word "[[wikt:integer|integer]]" in abstract algebra.}} Namely, <math>\mathbb{Z}=O_{\mathbb{Q}}</math> where <math>\mathbb{Q}</math> is the [[Field (mathematics)|field]] of [[rational number]]s.{{sfn|Cassels|1986|p=192}}  And indeed, in [[algebraic number theory]] the elements of <math>\mathbb{Z}</math> are often called the "rational integers" because of this.

The next simplest example is the ring of [[Gaussian integer]]s <math>\mathbb{Z}[i]</math>, consisting of [[complex number]]s whose [[real and imaginary parts]] are integers. It is the ring of integers in the number field <math>\mathbb{Q}(i)</math> of [[Gaussian rational]]s, consisting of complex numbers whose real and imaginary parts are rational numbers. Like the rational integers, <math>\mathbb{Z}[i]</math> is a [[Euclidean domain]]. 

The ring of integers of an algebraic number field is the unique maximal [[order (ring theory)|order]] in the field. It is always a [[Dedekind domain]].{{sfn|Samuel|1972|p=49}}

== Properties ==
The ring of integers {{math|size=120%|O<sub>''K''</sub>}} is a [[finitely-generated module|finitely-generated]] <math>\mathbb Z</math>-[[module (mathematics)|module]].  Indeed, it is a [[free module|free]] <math>\mathbb Z</math>-module, and thus has an '''integral basis''', that is a [[basis (linear algebra)|basis]] {{math|size=120%|''b''<sub>1</sub>, ..., ''b''<sub>''n''</sub> ∈ O<sub>''K''</sub>}} of the <math>\mathbb Q</math>-[[vector space]]&nbsp;{{mvar|K}} such that each element&nbsp;{{mvar|x}} in {{math|size=120%|O<sub>''K''</sub>}} can be uniquely represented as
:<math>x=\sum_{i=1}^na_ib_i,</math>
with <math>a_i \in \mathbb Z</math>.<ref name=Cas193>Cassels (1986) p. 193</ref>  The [[rank of a free module|rank]]&nbsp;{{mvar|n}} of {{math|size=120%|O<sub>''K''</sub>}} as a free <math>\mathbb Z</math>-module is equal to the [[Degree of a field extension|degree]] of&nbsp;{{mvar|K}} over <math>\mathbb Q</math>.

==Examples==

=== Computational tool ===
A useful tool for computing the integral closure of the ring of integers in an algebraic field <math>K / \mathbb Q</math> is the [[Discriminant of an algebraic number field|discriminant]]. If {{math|''K''}} is of degree {{math|''n''}} over <math>\mathbb Q</math>, and <math>\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_n \in \mathcal{O}_K</math> form a basis of <math>K</math> over <math>\mathbb Q</math>, set <math>d = \Delta_{K/\mathbb{Q}}(\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_n)</math>. Then, <math>\mathcal{O}_K</math> is a [[submodule]] of the {{nowrap|<math>\mathbb Z</math>-module}} spanned by <math>\alpha_1/d,\ldots,\alpha_n/d</math>.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web|url=http://people.math.gatech.edu/~mbaker/pdf/ANTBook.pdf|title=Algebraic Number Theory|last=Baker|pages=33–35}}</ref> <sup>pg. 33</sup> In fact, if {{math|''d''}} is square-free, then <math>\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_n</math> forms an integral basis for <math>\mathcal{O}_K</math>.<ref name=":0" /> <sup>pg. 35</sup>

=== Cyclotomic extensions ===
If {{mvar|p}} is a [[prime number|prime]], {{math|''ζ''}}&nbsp;is a {{mvar|p}}th [[root of unity]] and <math>K = \mathbb Q(\zeta)</math> is the corresponding [[cyclotomic field]], then an integral basis of <math>\mathcal{O}_K=\mathbb{Z}[\zeta]</math> is given by {{math|size=120%|(1, ''ζ'', ''ζ''<sup>&thinsp;2</sup>, ..., ''ζ''<sup>&thinsp;''p''−2</sup>)}}.{{sfn|Samuel|1972|p=43}}

=== Quadratic extensions ===
If <math>d</math> is a [[square-free integer]] and <math>K = \mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{d}\,)</math> is the corresponding [[quadratic field]], then <math>\mathcal{O}_K</math> is a ring of [[quadratic integer]]s and its integral basis is given by <math>\left(1, \frac{1 + \sqrt{d}}{2}\right)</math> if {{math|''d'' ≡ 1 ([[Modular arithmetic|mod]] 4)}} and by <math>(1, \sqrt{d})</math> if {{math|''d'' ≡ 2, 3 (mod 4)}}.{{sfn|Samuel|1972|p=35}} This can be found by computing the [[Minimal polynomial (field theory)|minimal polynomial]] of an arbitrary element <math>a + b\sqrt{d} \in \mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{d})</math> where <math>a,b \in \mathbb{Q}</math>.

==Multiplicative structure==
In a ring of integers, every element has a factorization into [[irreducible element]]s, but the ring need not have the property of [[Unique factorization domain|unique factorization]]: for example, in the ring of integers <math>\mathbb Z[\sqrt{-5}]</math>, the element 6 has two essentially different factorizations into irreducibles:{{sfn|Samuel|1972|p=49}}<ref>{{cite book|last=Artin|first=Michael|title=Algebra|date=2011|publisher=Prentice Hall|isbn=978-0-13-241377-0|page=360}}</ref>
:<math> 6 = 2 \cdot 3 = (1 + \sqrt{-5})(1 - \sqrt{-5}).</math>

A ring of integers is always a [[Dedekind domain]], and so has unique factorization of [[ideal (ring theory)|ideals]] into [[prime ideal]]s.{{sfn|Samuel|1972|p=50}}

The [[Unit (ring theory)|units]] of a ring of integers {{math|''O''<sub>''K''</sub>}} form a [[finitely generated abelian group]] by [[Dirichlet's unit theorem]].  The [[torsion subgroup]] consists of the [[roots of unity]] of {{math|''K''}}.  A set of torsion-free generators is called a set of ''[[Fundamental unit (number theory)|fundamental units]]''.{{sfn|Samuel|1972|pp=59–62}}

==Generalization==
One defines the ring of integers of a [[non-archimedean local field]] {{math|''F''}} as the set of all elements of {{math|''F''}} with absolute value {{math|≤&thinsp;1}}; this is a ring because of the strong triangle inequality.{{sfn|Cassels|1986|p=41}}  If {{math|''F''}} is the completion of an algebraic number field, its ring of integers is the completion of the latter's ring of integers.  The ring of integers of an algebraic number field may be characterised as the elements which are integers in every non-archimedean completion.{{sfn|Cassels|1986|p=192}}

For example, the [[p-adic integer|{{mvar|p}}-adic integers]] <math>\mathbb Z_p</math> are the ring of integers of the [[p-adic number|{{mvar|p}}-adic numbers]] <math>\mathbb Q_p</math>.
